newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada seen resisting rate hike pressure.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada seen resisting rate hike pressure.

text.p: The Bank of Canada will resist market pressures to raise short-term interest rates unless the Canadian dollar plummets in value, economists said on Friday.
Analysts said Canada's central bank did not want to jeopardize the country's economic recovery by raising rates, although its stand was clearly hurting the Canadian dollar.

"The Bank of Canada and the markets are in a standoff right now, with markets pushing the currency down in the wake of Fed tightening," said Anita Lauria, an economist with Salomon Brothers in New York.

Canada's dollar closed at a two-year low of C$1.3925 (US$0.7181) on Thurday and weakened further in Friday's session. The currency's weakness in the past two weeks prompted the Bank of Canada to intervene several times on financial markets, buying Canadian dollars to slow its fall.

But analysts said the Bank of Canada would resist hiking short-term rates to defend the currency unless there was a pickup in the size and speed of the currency's depreciation, with the dollar moving past the C$1.40 (US$0.7143) level, "As long as the currency doesn't go into a free fall, I don't see any scope for them to raise rates. We still have a huge output gap," said Dan Kelly, director of financial markets research with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc. "I don't think they mind a little depreciation in the currency."

Canada's dollar began weakening sharply ahead of last week's rate hike by the U.S. Federal Reserve. It fell further as strong U.S. economic reports prompted speculation the Fed would hike again in May.
Investors fear a widening differential between Canadian and U.S. short-term rates will prompt more selling of the currency.

Canada's key bank rate is at a 35-year low of 3.25 percent, well below the U.S. federal funds rate of 5.5 percent. The Bank of Canada last year began charting a "made in Canada" interest rate policy, cutting rates 11 times versus just one cut by the Fed.

Pressure is therefore growing on the Bank of Canada to match last week's U.S. rate hike in order to defend the dollar. Such a move would attract capital flows back into Canada and strengthen the currency.

The Bank of Canada is resisting that pressure because there appears to be little domestic need to raise rates. Despite some indications that economic growth is picking up, inflation is below 2.0 percent and the gap between potential output and demand remains high.
"They just started getting a recovery going that's absorbing slack," said Lauria. "Is there a domestic justification for rate hikes? The answer has to be no."

Many investors had expected the Bank of Canada to hike rates this morning after a report showing stronger than expected Canadian job growth. Adding to the impetus was a U.S. employment report suggesting inflation there may be accelerating.
Two main factors were helping the Bank of Canada withstand the pressure to raise rates, analysts said.

T-bill yields and other short-term interest rates set on the open market have spiked higher, providing a defacto tightening of monetary conditions in Canada, noted Josh Mendelsohn, chief economist with Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.
Foreign reserves, which the Bank of Canada uses to defend the currency, are also near all-time highs. The Finance Department on Thursday reported reserves rose to US$21.64 billion in March.

Some analysts said the central bank may be playing a dangerous game by holding rates steady in the face of a weakening currency. If the Canadian dollar was allowed to weaken sharply, it might take more than a single rate hike to strengthen it.

"The easiest thing that you can predict right now is where the currency will go. Each day that the Bank of Canada doesn't tighten, you'll see further weakness in the currency," said Andrew Pyle, head of fixed-income research with ABN AMRO Bank Canada.
